title: The Ballad of Jack and Rose
full_review:
Despite fine performances, and a few good scenes, there's no escaping the fact that "The Ballad of Jack and Rose" (IFC) is an offbeat, slow-moving film.

Daniel Day-Lewis plays a nonconformist with a bad heart condition who lives alone with his teenage daughter (Camilla Belle) on a former island commune "off the East Coast of the United States," sheltering the girl from as much of the outside world as possible.

But perhaps fearing that they're becoming too close, he decides to bring the woman he has been dating (Catherine Keener) into the house, along with the woman's two teenage sons, disrupting the delicate balance of their solitary lifestyle.

All the while, he fends off the encroachments of a real estate developer (Beau Bridges) at odds with his own environmental outlook.

Written and directed by Rebecca (daughter of late playwright Arthur) Miller, the disjointed film features an accomplished portrayal by her real-life husband, the always watchable Day-Lewis. Though Miller creates an atmospheric backdrop for her strange tale, the vaguely incestuous undertones between father and daughter and a scene where the daughter invites one of the boys to deflower her make for fitfully distasteful viewing.

The film contains some rough and crude language, sexual situations and innuendo, a brief incestuous kiss, some talk of suicide, partial nudity, and some drug material. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
